title: Roman denarius/siliquae hoards from Gudme, Funen, Denmark
language_note: National Museum of Denmark record, English-language version used here; Danish original also available at the same institution.
date: settlement flourished 3rd-7th century CE; the Gudme III hoard's coins are 4th-century CE Roman silver siliquae
findspot: Gudme, southeast Funen (Fyn), Denmark, with an associated trading site at nearby Lundeborg
original_text_excerpt: Gudme III: a hoard of 293 Roman silver coins (siliquae) from the 4th century AD. A related treasure included nine gold bracteates, a small sword stud with garnets in cloisonne, a finger ring, two round pendants and a worn Roman silver denarius.
original_text_note: Summarized from the National Museum of Denmark's 'Gudme - gold, gods and people' exhibition text.
notes: Gudme was one of Iron Age Denmark's largest and wealthiest settlements (a magnate's farm plus ~50 smaller farms) and shows the clearest concentration of Roman silver coinage in Scandinavia, alongside Dankirke in Jutland. Roman denarii/siliquae at these sites are read by scholars as markers of political centrality and foreign-trade connections rather than ordinary circulating currency — worth flagging that nuance in any grounded answer.
